newsitem.title: UK: UK's Cook says jobs must balance EMU targets.
newsitem.headline: UK's Cook says jobs must balance EMU targets.

text.p: Britain's new Labour government said on Wednesday that the pursuit of a single European currency should be balanced with broader economic objectives such as higher employment.

Foreign Secretary Robin Cook told a Trades Union Congress (TUC) conference on the social dimensions of European integration that the people of Europe needed to see that EU membership was of benefit to them.
The new government supported the inclusion of an employment chapter in the European Union treaty at next month's EU summit in Amsterdam, he said.

"We will do so because we believe that it is very important that we should balance the monetary targets that are already in the treaty relating to the single currency with broader economic objectives such as higher levels of employment," Cook said.
"Progress towards achieving those monetary targets must be within an overall package that's aimed at creating jobs and must not be at the expense of employment."
Cook's remarks on the importance of jobs echoed those of TUC general Secretary John Monks, who told the conference:
"Governments must realise that, to advance on Europe, their citizens will want to see a Europe that can deliver on jobs."
But Cook made no reference to Monks's call for the so-called "convergence criteria" for joining the single currency to be interpreted flexibly.
The union chief said the European Union had focussed too much on maintaining financial stability and not enough on jobs.
"The criteria are reference values, not precise commandments," he added.

The foreign secretary said the Labour government had already achieved a substantial improvement in the climate at EU negotiations by making clear that, unlike its Conservative predecessor, it would not simply "heckle from the sidelines."

There would be hard bargaining at the summit, but he was hopeful of an agreement covering issues of key importance for Britain such as control of its external borders and retaining national vetos in foreign policy and other areas.
Cook said he did not accept that signing up to the Social Chapter on workers' rights, which the new government plans to do, would damage Britain's competitiveness, but added:
"We will carefully scrutinise all future directives to make sure that they will boost employment rather than hinder employment."

Looking ahead to Britain's six-month presidency of the 15-nation bloc in the first half of 1998, Cook said a high priority would be to ensure a "level playing field" in industries such as telecommunications, financial services and energy.
Britain was strong in these sectors and including them in the EU's single market would be in the interest of employment here.
Britain's other main priority for its presidency would be enlargement of the EU to include former communist countries in central and eastern Europe.

Asked to elaborate on his ambitions for Britain to play a leading role in the EU alongside France and Germany, Cook said he had not meant this in the sense of a commanding officer, leading troops from the front.
It was more a question of "shaping the agenda, influencing the direction."
"For 18 years we have sat in the back seat and complained about where we were being driven. I want a Britain up there helping to choose the direction."
